name: Mouk-Aria
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Thurston, William R. 1996, The Bibling Languages of Northwestern New Britain, in Ross (ed.), Pacific Linguistics C-135, pp. 249-392 (grammar sketch per Glottolog); not open-access

new_statements.quote: The syllabic canon of the Bibling languages is (C1) V (C2), where C1 can be any consonant, most sequences of stop + resonant, or the sequence sl; where V can be any vowel; and where C2 can be any consonant. Stress tends to be penultimate. Resonants in clusters after voiceless stops tend to be voiceless. [p. 253] ... In addition, all languages permit a word-initial syllabic nasal that never occurs with stress. [p. 254] || Thurston 1987:34: Stress patterns in running speech have not been worked out in detail for most of the languages, but for words pronounced in isolation, stress is usually penultimate in all languages.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (144 pp., ANU Open Research bitstream; chapter footer gives DOI 10.15144/PL-C135.249 and 'Online edition licensed 2015 CC BY-SA 4.0'). PDF page 5 = printed p. 253, header 'THE BIBLING LANGUAGES OF NORTHWESTERN NEW BRITAIN 253', §2 PHONOLOGY (section opens on p. 252). The quoted passage is there verbatim (extracted text and the rendered page image both checked): 'The syllabic canon of the Bibling languages is (C1) V (C2), where C1 can be any consonant, most sequences of stop + resonant, or the sequence sl; where V can be any vowel; and where C2 can be any consonant. Stress tends to be penultimate. Resonants in clusters after voiceless stops tend to be voiceless.' PDF page 6 = p. 254,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable (1996: 'tends to be'; 1987: 'usually', for words pronounced in isolation). A word-initial syllabic nasal (e.g. Mouk mgux [m̩gux] 'howl', Aria mluk [m̩luk] 'hit') is never stressed. The 1996 examples mark stress with an acute on the penult (Mouk áikos 'widower', lánae 'he wants', sláŋa 'his ear'; Aria óbar 'pig', émris 'you bathe'; the 1987 example Mouk básex 'pour').
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as a tendency ('tends to be' / 'usually'); word-initial syllabic nasals never carry stress; running-speech stress patterns explicitly stated as not worked out (1987:34).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, words in isolation (1987 says so explicitly). The 1996 statement is made for the Bibling languages collectively (Mouk, Aria, Tourai = Mouk-Aria [mwh]; plus Lamogai [lmg], lamo1243), not for Mouk-Aria alone; the 1987 statement covers all NWNB languages (Anêm, Mouk, Aria, Tourai, Lamogai, Lusi, Kove, Kabana, Kilenge/Maleu, Amara). Data collected by Thurston 1981-82 in Mouk, Aria, Tourai villages.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog mouk1239 = Mouk-Aria [mwh], covering the varieties Thurston calls Mouk (Mok), Aria and Tourai. Both statements are group-level: Thurston 1996 speaks of 'the Bibling languages' (Mouk, Aria, Tourai, Lamogai — the last is Lamogai [lmg], lamo1243, a separate Glottolog language), and Thurston 1987 of 'all languages' of NWNB. The 1996 chapter's example words with marked penultimate stress are mostly Mouk and Aria, so the statement applies to mouk1239 directly, but no Mouk-specific vs Aria-specific stress statement exists.
